en: He was battered by the steel-bearing foe
He told the news at once
When great Kiten heard this
Strength left his very core
Shouting to the champions
Stirring earth and sky
Growing wrathful and straining
The champion who brought the news
The khan raged like a beast
The warrior’s condition was dire
The champions were wrathful at heart
Who heard these words of yours
For this, from seven distant lands
The land received the report
It was a pitch-dark night
This was a bloody calamity
The lone Burut had caused ruin
What deed was this that brought destruction
What could be taken from the great quarrel
What did they mean by Kumayt
Do not ask how far Bilgich had come,
Beijing is no trifling land,
Great Bilgich is no common warrior,
To the champion who came with news,
When told to speak, three valiant men,
Barely entered among you,
Saying Beijing's chief had grown obstinate,
Saying it was the ill-fated Bilgich himself,
Standing there, he spoke the truth,
He told of the moment disaster struck,
How an enclosure closed around Bilgich,
While no Burut remained behind,
How they died before the khan,
Asking how such a thing had happened,
The khan of Kakan spoke of the champion,
Kulchoro rode among the warriors,
Asking what sort of enemy had trapped them,
That honored champion was like this,
All of them had gone out as marksmen,
His strength as a champion was extraordinary,
His heroism was beyond measure,
When he clashed, none could withstand him,
When he fought, no enemy defeated him,
He surrendered no companion to anyone,
From his core he was truly fierce,
No champion emerged alive,
They said that Burut youth was the one,
They said wounded Bilgich remained,
Breaking China's back,
He brought peace to the Kyrgyz souls,
He stilled the souls of the Chinese,
Among the Chinese above all,
He found no champion at all,
What could you find that equaled him?
One champion speaks a champion's words,
At his majesty they murmur,
To the champion awaiting news,
The battle inflicted upon the champions,
As though he had become a scourge to champions,
The force he sent was living men,
As if defending against encirclement,
He cried out in his fury,
Behind his shield stood his khan,
The champion before the khan,
What kind of raider was he in action?
When the khan struck the Burut,
He did not turn back amid the blood,
If fate allowed, what a raider he was,
The champion who struck the multitude,
With news reaching his khan,
The finest of his kind,
Beside the one worn down,
When he arrived bearing the news,
To the dark host standing there,
Saying five champions had lost their lives,
To those standing under his command,
He spoke before the assembly,
He issued an order and sent them,
Though one wing had been shattered,
When he looked at Bilgich,
What could poor Kite do?
Turning his dawn into misery darker than night,
Turning what he had arranged into turmoil,
Now God had struck Kite,
While the people of Kakan looked on,
Rejoicing over the wretched Burut,
So that Beijing could no longer boast,
Saying it had now been devastated,
There remained a single cauldron,
When dawn broke the next day,
They brought eighty oxen at a time,
And slaughtered them with force,
He had the funeral feast served in Kakan,
He made a mighty commotion,
After the rites, he was laid to rest,
They brought great Kite,
He asked who had gone out to the combat,
From the khan's place to the field,
He sat restoring his composure,
His form and outward appearance,
Had terrified the khan's people,
At the great gate known to the people,
Through the great gate, great Bilgich,
Leaving no count of the deeds recounted,
His life from battle was thus,
One slipped away after matching him,
Another remained behind him,
Of the khanly people of Black China,
The Kalmyks fell into turmoil like grain,
He entered before Khan Kite,
His fine mustache bristling,
Great Bilgich, tormented and ill,
As though about to depart for the other world,
No one could stand before his suffering.
It cools, softly murmuring,
There is no equal to the hero’s eyes.
From the singular form of the warrior,
Weary with hardship, he closed his eyes,
A fluid grace flowed as he rode,
Like a thirsty thoroughbred hero advancing,
Before him was something that barely touched the ground,
His appearance differed from that of men,
His weight and bearing were exceptional,
He could assail a multitude of men,
There was a light at his fetlock,
As though even a mountain would not stir,
The blue-maned one seemed to tower proudly,
His stride was unlike that of a sheep,
If the blue khan now sent many,
If the enemy came in force behind shields,
Even in numbers they could not take him,
If many set upon him from behind,
Why would you not go straight at them?
He was of a fierce disposition,
In battle he would brook no distinction,
I shall know you well,
When I speak, my words are clear,
In this world, keen-sighted,
By his father’s measure, the warrior is lofty,
Now his manifest strength,
If the thoroughbred came against the foe,
Now to scatter the white bellies,
Seeing his majesty, they were frightened,
When I looked at his two eyes,
They were like pits dug in the open field,
When I looked at his nose,
Like the slope of a rugged mountain,
His two eyes were exceptional,
His two sides were like bedding laid out,
His ribs were a solid shield,
The hero’s aspect was like a broad hollow.
No crow dared confront him,
No croaking raven flew there,
It became a desert that boiled the brain,
It became land they had traversed,
They grappled in a great struggle,
They remained warm-backed,
Taking a giant as vast as ninety tracts,
Twisting about, unable to find a way,
Like a poor, bewildered child,
Seeing the bay horse’s fat as a coat,
Ak Joltoy proved superior,
Every part of him was like a host of troops,
The wicked giant [?],
The mace tore across his face,
That warrior Ak Joltoy,
Without yielding beneath the sun,
Fighting day and night,
Shouting, those champions mounted,
Joltoy had fallen behind,
The many horses taken from the Burut,
He had stayed there guarding them without leaving,
With the prosperous household,
With the unfortunate hero Kairy,
With the mighty champion-warrior,
They had continued without being able to prevail,
Preparing Jardyger’s army,
The champion Jayy was there,
The hero’s valiant son arrived,
Kulansur and Kuluker
The charger had suffered
For four days without rest
Sitting after making one victory known
If the separated thousands were true
Saying he passed ahead of them
The two chargers surged
The horses’ labor numbered in thousands
Straining along the road
If the road led toward China
He led the road without delay
Against the mass of enemies
His people were separated between them
He returned again to Talas
Keeping the court and becoming khan
Alive in thirty places
Taking a letter from the Kalmyks
Traveling through many lands
His thoughts divided among the people
He was named the hero Kenen
Pouring blood into the black water
Setting fire to the land of booty
Traveling and gathering lions
The Chinese awaited warriors
Counting their strength, they broke apart
Their countless treasure was exhausted
Sating them with yellow gold
Enriching them with brown horses
All that belonged to Kulansur
Mounting the blue Altai horse
Keeping the charger ready
Becoming known to the ancestral people
Would any person face him
When mighty Kiten heard this
After hearing news from Bilgich
His eyes filled with tears
Gathering the Kalmyks and preparing
It was a grief to thousands
The people were pledged to sorrow
When several years had passed
From Kakan who ruled the Chinese
Gathering his great host
Of the Chinese in motley coats
A harsh burden befell them
Against the wretched Burut
To bring about his end
No man could reach him
A tiger descended to play
No warrior dared go
No warrior remained on the march
Give account to all Beijing
You will take the great bellows
With a horse swift as the moon
He had a messenger found
Forty thousand of Beijing
He had the great gate opened
To populous Beijing
Let us send the true report
The widowed women fixed their eyes
Let us proclaim it through Beijing
Frightening all the people
From the force hidden from sight
His court turned to ruin
Without sparing the women of Kakan
From where arrows flew by tens
Leaving no maiden in Beijing
Let us gather the thousands around
If they are not satisfied by the spoken word
If they do not yield before it
Forty tribes from forty thousand
Purifying it every dawn
To sit upon the throne
To rule over the Chinese people
What the people knew in the end
Let us send word to appoint him
More precious than spoken counsel
Let us send news that it was given
